papers.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
papers.abstract: Asked to name a running shoe brand, language models say Nike. Asked to recommend one, they say Brooks. This paper asks where models learn that taste. Across 102 models and 42 brand categories, the brand a model picks when recommending differs from the brand it names in 26. The field moves together to a shared recommendation. The Named brands are market leaders, and the Picked brands are mostly niche and specialist. Three open training pipelines show where this forms. Pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to answer and mostly leaves the pick unchanged. Preference optimization (DPO) teaches the model which answer is better, and the pick moves in all three pipelines, by 11 to 24 points. The preference data contains almost no brands. DPO moves the model's judgments toward a second set of associations even when the preferred brand is not in the preference data, and the effect reaches beyond brands. Asked to choose a sauce, models switch from ketchup to pesto. We do not know exactly how these preferences arise. We suspect they come from the judge models that decide which answers count as better during preference training. For brands, a recommendation depends less on what a model knows about them than on whether they fit this taste.
papers.summary: Ask LLMs to "name a running shoe brand" and they will most likely say Nike; ask them to "recommend a running shoe brand" and they are more likely to say Brooks. The paper measures this effect across 102 models and 42 categories. In 26 categories the answer changes this way, and the models move together to the same brand: Chrome becomes Firefox, Google becomes DuckDuckGo. The brands named off the cuff are mostly market leaders; the brands picked after some thought are mostly niche or specialist ones. Tracing back through the training stages, the author finds the key step is preference training, even though the training data for that step hardly mentions brands.

deep_reading.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
deep_reading.content:
Ask a language model to "name a running shoe brand" and it will most likely say Nike; ask it to "recommend a running shoe brand" and it is more likely to say Brooks. This paper measures that effect across 102 models and 42 categories. When a model is first asked for recommendations and then asked to pick one, the "panel answer" (the brand all models give most often) differs from the "name one" answer in 26 categories. And the models do not each drift somewhere different; **they move together to the same brand**: Delta becomes Singapore Airlines, Chrome becomes Firefox, Google becomes DuckDuckGo. The brands named off the cuff are mostly market leaders; the brands picked after some thought are mostly niche or specialist ones. The author then asks at which training step this "taste" appears. Using three open models that publish their weights after every training stage, they find the key step is preference training: ==in the step where the model learns which of two answers is better, the pick moves by 11 to 24 percentage points==, even though the data used in that step hardly mentions brands.

![The paper's Table 1: from naming to picking (102 models, 42 categories). The "consensus moved" column counts categories where the panel's most common answer differs from its answer to "name one", and it grows down the table; the "answer unchanged" column is the share of a model's answers that are still the brand it names itself, falling from 89% to 31%.](figs/2610.28272/crop_tab1.png)

## 1. The problem: where do the brands a model recommends come from?

More and more people simply ask an AI assistant to "recommend one". Existing audits look at which brands production assistants recommend and whether the answer holds up when the question is reworded; few ask which training step put those preferences there. The paper starts from a simple contrast: "name one" asks what the model thinks of first, while "recommend one" asks it to make a judgment for the user. If the two answers differ, the model is not judging by "who is most famous" but by a different set of associations.

## 2. How the experiment works: four ways of asking about the same category, put to 102 models

The author picked 42 categories, from soda to cloud providers, and asked about each one in several ways to see whether the answer changes. The first three are a single question that tells the model to reply with one name only; below we call them the one-name questions:

- "Name": name a running shoe brand.
- "Choose": choose a running shoe brand.
- "Recommend": can you recommend a running shoe brand?

The fourth is the two-turn question. In one conversation the model is first asked "Can you recommend a running shoe brand?" and usually lists three to five; it is then asked "Which one would you pick?" and has to choose one from its own list. The brand from this turn is called the Picked brand below. Going from "Name" to the two-turn question, the request moves step by step from "what comes to mind first" to "make the call for me", and the author wants to see how the answer changes along that line.

All 102 models are called through OpenRouter, a service that reaches many vendors' models through one interface. The "temperature" is set to 1. Temperature controls how random the answers are: at 0, a model always gives the answer it rates most likely, so asking again changes nothing; at 1, it draws an answer according to its own probabilities. If it gives Nike 70% and Brooks 30% (illustrative), ten asks yield roughly seven Nikes and three Brookses. What gets measured is therefore each model's whole spread of preferences, not only its single most common answer. Because answers are drawn at random, each question is repeated: 8 times per model and category for the one-name questions and 4 times for the two-turn question.

Twenty-five models can either "write some internal thinking before answering" or "answer directly"; the author also ran each of them with thinking switched off, so both modes are in the data. Perplexity's Sonar is left out because it searches the web before answering, so it would measure search results, not the model's own preference. Data were collected between 30 September and 10 October 2026, and since vendors keep updating their models, the conclusions describe the versions served in that window.

## 3. How a reply is mapped to a brand

The one-name questions ask for a single name, so only a clean single name counts. "Brooks" is counted; "I'd recommend Brooks because…", which adds a lead-in, or a list of several brands is not.

In the two-turn question the second reply is usually a paragraph. The author extracts the brand the model finally says it would choose: "These are all good, but if I had to pick one I'd go with Brooks" is recorded as Brooks. Sometimes the second reply is still just a list, or asks the user back, "Do you mostly run on roads or trails?", or declines to choose for the user; all of these count as no pick. No pick happens in 17% of two-turn replies, and later shares are computed only over replies that do pick a brand. Variant spellings and product names of one brand are merged into that brand.

The mapping is done by a program. The author hand-checked three samples, and the human reading agreed with the program on 87% to 97% of replies. In other words, the program occasionally gets one wrong, but rarely enough that it does not change the conclusions.

## 4. Finding one: the name that comes to mind is the leader, the considered pick is someone else

Start with the overall trend in Table 1. The more the question looks like "make the call for the user", the more categories change their panel answer: out of 42, "Choose" changes 6, "Recommend" changes 16, and the two-turn question changes 26, more than half. Individual models behave the same way. For each model, take the brand it most often gives when asked to "name" one; on average, 89% of a model's answers to "name" are that brand, which shows it is very stable when answering off the cuff; in the two-turn question, only 31% of its picks are still that brand. ==Once the question changes, the models do not scatter; they move together to a new consensus==.

![The paper's Table 2: the 26 categories where the Picked brand differs from the Named brand. Each row shows, from left to right, the panel's most common brand under the four questions; in most categories the brand only changes in the "recommend" or two-turn column.](figs/2610.28272/crop_tab2.png)

The brands named off the cuff are market leaders such as Google, Walmart, McDonald's, Facebook and Verizon. The picks are mostly smaller brands with a good reputation among insiders, such as DuckDuckGo, Aldi, Sierra Nevada, Reddit, Signal and Brooks; a few are more upmarket, such as Hermès over Chanel and Hyatt over Marriott.

The models do not throw out the brand they named; they just move it down. In the two-turn question, that brand appears in the model's own recommendation list 83% of the time, Among only the lists that include it, 60% put it first, yet just 37% end up picking it (counting the cases where it is not listed, the pick rate is 31%). Lists vary in length, with a median of 4 brands; drawing one at random from each list at its actual length would pick it about 30% of the time on average. Being listed first therefore gives it almost no advantage: the model votes for another brand on the list, and different models vote for the same one. Nor is this one lab's quirk: in each of the 12 labs with at least 3 models tested, the two-turn question changes that lab's consensus brand in 55% to 74% of categories.

Two side observations. First, labs favour their own AI assistant: asked to "recommend an AI assistant", Anthropic's models answer Claude 92% of the time, while other labs' models answer Claude 15% of the time. The favouritism does not extend to other products; Google's models recommend Google search and Chrome less often than other labs' models do. Second, the author spot-checked Claude Opus 5.5 with web search switched on. It answered the two-turn question without searching once, and its picks largely matched the panel, which suggests that production assistants also rely mainly on the model's own preferences for this kind of recommendation.

## 5. Finding two: taste forms in the step that learns "which answer is better"

To find the step where taste appears, one needs the same model's version after each training stage. A chat model typically goes through pretraining (giving the base model), SFT, DPO and RL, in that order.

OLMo 3 7B, OLMo 3.1 32B and Tulu 3 8B are open models that publish their weights after every step, while Nemotron 3.5 Lightning publishes only a base and a final version. For this part the author stops drawing repeated samples and reads directly the probability the model assigns to each brand name. One read tells how much the model wants to say that brand, so every stage can be measured on every category.

The first step looks at pretraining. A base model cannot yet answer "please recommend one", but it can finish half a sentence. Given the half-sentence "If you want a good web browser, I recommend", Tulu's base model continues with Firefox in 13 of 20 draws; given "A well-known web browser is", it continues with Chrome in 10. Across the 16 categories where the recommended brand differs from the named one, switching to advice phrasing raises the recommended brand's share in 7 to 10 categories and lowers it in at most 1. This shows that the brand picked later does not come from nowhere: ==in the text seen during pretraining, it already tends to appear next to words like "recommend"==.

The second step compares SFT with DPO. The author gives every stage the same multiple-choice question: a list of three brands, namely the named brand, the picked brand and another frequently recommended brand, followed by "Which one would you pick?". To read probabilities directly, the reply is made to start with "I'd pick", and the author checks which brand the model is most likely to put next. Base models tend to favour the first item, so each list is shown in forward and reverse order and the two results are averaged.

| Model | Base | SFT | DPO | RL | SFT→DPO (90% interval) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| OLMo 3 7B | 58% | 52% | 76% | 74% | +24 [+16, +33] |
| Tulu 3 8B | 54% | 58% | 69% | 68% | +11 [+6, +16] |
| OLMo 3.1 32B | 63% | 57% | 73% | 73% | +16 [+7, +25] |

The table looks only at the probabilities of the named and the picked brand: the picked brand's share of their sum (the third brand is left out), averaged first over the two list orders and then over the 26 categories where the two differ. 50% would be a tie. After SFT all three models are still near their base level; after DPO all three rise clearly, and RL mostly keeps what DPO set. The brackets in the last column are a 90% interval, i.e. the range the rise moves within when the author resamples the categories many times. All three intervals are above zero, which shows the rise is not driven by a handful of categories. Nemotron has no intermediate versions and rises from 58% at base to 79% in its final version.

Which brands exactly does DPO lift? Across all 42 categories, the author compares two things: how likely the base model is to name a brand off the cuff, and how much DPO raises that brand when the model recommends. The more readily a brand is named off the cuff, the less DPO lifts it, in all three models. So **DPO lifts the brands the base model found less obvious**. But DPO does not push down famous brands across the board: in the 16 categories where the panel already recommends the famous brand, that brand does not fall after DPO. Since a three-item multiple-choice question is an artificial setup, the author re-ran the test on the SFT model's own recommendation lists, and the DPO step still adds 9 to 14 percentage points.

## 6. Finding three: the training data hardly mentions brands; the taste may come from the models that grade answers

The training data of OLMo 3 and Tulu 3 are public. The author searched them for requests that mention one of the 26 categories together with words like "recommend", "best" or "which". OLMo 3's DPO data has 260,000 pairs; the better answer names the picked brand only 3 times and the worse answer once, and Tulu 3 is just as sparse. So DPO did not learn these picks from brand examples, although indirect associations elsewhere in the data cannot be ruled out.

The same change appears outside brands. The author used a set of everyday categories, such as a tree, a smell or an animal, and compared "name one" with "choose one". Base models barely tell the two questions apart; after DPO, all three models lean toward the panel's answer when asked to "choose one". The clearest case is sauce: asked to choose a sauce, OLMo 3 7B picks pesto 5% of the time at base, 27% after SFT and 67% after DPO, while ketchup falls from 72% to 6%.

So who decides which answer is better? Half of OLMo 3's DPO data is graded by a large model acting as judge; the other half simply treats Qwen 3 32B's answer as the better one and a much smaller model's answer as the worse one. Tulu 3's pairs are graded by GPT-4o. The author therefore suspects the taste is passed on from these judge models. Tulu 3 has a single judge, GPT-4o, which allows a test: take the categories where GPT-4o recommends a different brand from the Tulu base model's favourite, put both brands in one list (asked in both orders), and ask the model before and after DPO which it picks. After DPO, the share picking GPT-4o's brand is 8 percentage points higher than before DPO, with a 90% interval of 2 to 14. This is only an approximate test, because the author queried today's GPT-4o, not the version that graded Tulu's data back then.

## 7. Limitations and what it means in practice

The author lists three main limitations. The questions are short and carry no personal context, so preferences measured on them may not reflect real use. The three models that can be inspected stage by stage come from the same organization and use similar training recipes, so the "DPO brings taste" path is shown only on them; the 102-model results, however, show the effect itself is not limited to these three. For OLMo 3 7B, if picks are sampled rather than read as probabilities, the change appears at RL instead of DPO. In addition, "judge models pass on taste" is the author's conjecture, and the 8 points on Tulu are only partial evidence. The author also notes that Claude Opus 5.5 was used to run probes, do the analysis and draft text, while Claude models are themselves among the subjects.

For post-training teams, the paper's warning is that ==preference training changes the model's judgments in areas its training data never covered, and the direction may come from the judge model==. If a product has a recommendation or choice step, such as a shopping assistant, local services or travel planning, it is worth running a set of "name one vs. recommend one" questions at every training stage, watching the change around DPO, and checking separately which brands the judge model itself favours. For brands, the author's conclusion is that whether a model recommends you depends more on whether you fit the model's implicit "taste" than on how much the model knows about you. How a brand can build that association is left to future work.

papers.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
papers.authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. deep_reading.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
deep_reading.content:
Two pairs of headphones have the same price, star rating and specs; one of them carries an extra line: "Our best-selling model, chosen by over 10,000 customers." Asked to pick one, GPT-4o picked the one with that line in 144 out of 144 trials. The authors then raised that product's price step by step. Only at about 13% more (about $17 on a $130 pair) did GPT-4o pick it just half the time. A plain, neutral product line, tested the same way, was also picked almost every time at equal price, but at about 2% more its share fell below half. By the usual "how often is it chosen" measure the two lines look identical; by "what is it worth" they differ six-fold. This paper from the University of Adelaide sets out to put such a price on every line a seller writes.

![Both lines are chosen almost 100% of the time at equal price; a price increase separates them: the plain line falls below half at about +2%, the strong "best-seller" line only at about +13%.](figs/2610.25843/hf2.png)

## 1. The problem: how much more can one seller sentence make a shopping agent pay

Large models are starting to act for users: browsing products, comparing, placing orders. A model that acts on someone's behalf is called an "agent". Once the decision-maker is a model rather than a person, sellers aim at a different target: a "best-seller" badge, an expert endorsement, or a reworded spec can all tilt an agent toward a product. The authors treat this as a **hidden discount**. Like a price cut it makes the product more likely to be chosen, but nothing changes on the price tag and the buyer cannot see it.

Earlier studies mostly report "after adding this line, the choice share rose by so much". That ruler has a flaw: any reasonably strong line pushes the share close to 100%, and beyond that it cannot show differences, like a ruler marked 0 to 100 cm trying to measure someone two metres tall. So "it raised the choice share" cannot answer the question that matters: is this line worth a few cents, or a large slice of the price?

## 2. Method: keep raising the price and see where it stops working

The authors call their approach a price-equivalent (PE for short below) audit, and the idea is direct. Each time the model sees two products with identical price, star rating, review count and specs; only one has an extra sentence at the end of its description. The paper calls that extra sentence a "cue". First the authors check how often the model picks the cued product at equal price, then they raise its price in steps: 2%, 4%, 6%, 8%, 12%, 18%, 26% more. The early steps are close together because most lines stop working after a small increase.

As the price rises, the share of trials in which the cued product is chosen keeps falling. Prices are tested only at a set of premiums from 0 to 26%; where the selection share drops from above half to below half between two adjacent premiums, the point of exactly half is interpolated on a straight line between them, and that premium is the line's PE. If a line has a PE of 13%, it means: this line makes the model willing to pay 13% more for the same thing, and any more than that it will not accept. Unlike the choice share, this ruler has no ceiling, so even strong lines can be ranked against each other.

Which of the two products is listed first also sways the model, as discussed later. To keep position out of the result, the authors put the cued product first half the time and second half the time, and attach the cue to product A half the time and to product B half the time.

In two situations no exact number can be measured, and the authors label them rather than forcing a value. In the first, the model already avoids the cued product at equal price, and raising the price only lowers its share further, so the PE can only be recorded as "at most 0". In the second, the model still picks the product at 26% more, so all that is known is "at least 26%". A number known only as an upper or lower bound like this is called "censored" in statistics, and it cannot be ranked directly against the others.

Each PE also comes with an error range (a 95% confidence interval, meaning that on this data the true value very likely lies inside it). The range is estimated like this: resample the 6 product pairs with replacement many times, recompute the PE each time, and see how much the result moves. This resampling method is called the bootstrap. The authors also warn that with only 6 pairs per category, the range may be too narrow.

The cues fall into several kinds:

- social proof, i.e. "lots of people bought it", at four strengths, from "very popular" to "our #1 best-selling model, chosen by over 100,000 customers";
- scarcity, "only a few left in stock";
- authority, "recommended by audio experts";
- rewordings that change the wording but not the information, such as a percentage written as a fraction, or the same fact told positively or negatively: "9 out of 10 buyers keep it" versus "1 out of 10 buyers returns it".

There were also controls: a plain product line, an empty line, and a neutral line matched in length to the persuasive line but with no persuasive content (to tell whether the effect comes from the content or merely from an extra line). The products were 6 pairs of headphones and 6 pairs of coffee makers. The models came from four companies, one strong and one weak from each, for example GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet and Haiku. Two models could not be used: Nova Pro failed to answer 21% of the time, and Llama-3.1-8B almost always picked whichever product came first, regardless of content. Every setting was asked 24 times per product pair and price point, 1,152 trials per cue, and 113,472 trials in total.

## 3. Main finding: what choice share cannot separate, price can

The authors plot every cue for GPT-4o on headphones on one chart: the x-axis is the choice share at equal price, the y-axis the PE.

![GPT-4o (headphones): x-axis is the choice share at equal price, y-axis the PE. Six lines are all chosen over 0.95 of the time at equal price, yet their PE ranges from 1.6% to 21.4%; "9 out of 10 keep it" has the highest PE while its equal-price share is actually lower.](figs/2610.25843/hf3.png)

Scarcity shows the problem most clearly. At equal price, "only a few left" is chosen 95% of the time, more than the 72% for "9 out of 10 buyers keep it". But once the price rises, scarcity's PE is only 1.6%, while "9 keep it" is at 22.3%, a 14-fold gap. Looking only at choice share ranks these two lines the wrong way round. The authors stress that running more trials would not fix this. The two quantities measure different things: one is how often the line wins at equal price, the other is how much price increase the line can absorb. Scarcity "wins often but tips over at a touch"; "9 keep it" "doesn't always win but holds up under price". Only the second kind is something a seller can turn into money.

The table gives the PE of the main lines on GPT-4o, that is, "what percentage of the price the line is worth":

| Line | Headphones | Coffee makers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Social proof: weak ("very popular") | 0.7 | 1.1 |
| Social proof: medium | 1.3 | 1.8 |
| Social proof: strong ("chosen by over 10,000") | 12.9 | 15.0 |
| Social proof: very strong ("#1, chosen by over 100,000") | 21.4 | 21.4 |
| Authority ("expert recommended", matching domain) | 19.8 | 21.6 |
| Scarcity ("only a few left") | 1.6 | 1.5 |
| "9 out of 10 keep it" | 22.3 | at least 26 |
| Plain product line | 2.0 | 1.5 |
| Percentage written as a fraction | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| Same-length line with no persuasive content | 10.6 | 11.2 |

Four things can be read from this table.

First, "lots of people bought it" does not work more the more strongly it is said; it switches on at a certain strength. "Very popular" and the medium version are worth almost nothing; at "chosen by over 10,000" the value jumps to about 13%. This also shows that PE really measures persuasion rather than noise.

Second, the same-length control line is also worth about 10%, more than the plain line. But the "very strong" version is clearly higher, so the extra part comes from what the line says, not just from adding a sentence.

Third, the model is completely unmoved by rewrites that convert numbers without changing information: a percentage written as a fraction has a PE of 0. Yet it reacts very differently to the same fact told positively (9 keep it) and negatively (1 returns it). In other words, **the model is moved by the form of a statement, not by the information itself**.

Fourth, authority only works when it fits. "Recommended by audio experts" is worth about 20% on headphones, but only about 1.9% on a coffee maker.

The authors also stacked social proof, authority and scarcity in pairs and all three together to test their combined effect. The result is roughly simple addition, with no sign of the lines amplifying or cancelling each other. With only 6 product pairs, though, a moderate interaction cannot be ruled out.

## 4. Do the findings hold with other models, positions and wordings

On the six models that took part properly, the "lots of people bought it" pattern holds: the weak and medium versions are at most 4%, the strong ones clearly higher; scarcity is at most 2% on every model. But at equal price the models take opposite views of scarcity: GPT-4o picks the "only a few left" product 95% of the time, Claude Sonnet only 19%, which looks more like an aversion.

PE cannot be used directly to rank models by "which is easier to sway", because it mixes two things: the pull of the line, and how sensitive the model is to price. At 10% more, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet and Llama-3.3-70B almost never pick the dearer identical product, while Nova Micro still does half the time. So when "expert recommended" is worth only 1.6% on Claude Sonnet, that does not mean it ignores such lines; it means it reacts quickly to price increases. Nova Micro still picks the cued product at more than double the price, so its PE cannot be measured at all; it looks "easy to fool" but simply does not care about price. The authors therefore advise that every audit also run a control with no cue at all, comparing price only, to first establish how price-sensitive the model is.

Being listed first has a price of its own. Across all trials GPT-4o chose the first-listed product 56% of the time, rising to about 65% when the signal was weak (only one product carried a cue, and its PE was below 3%). The authors priced "being first" as if it were a cue, using the price-only control with no cues: how much the first-listed product's price must rise before the share choosing it falls to one half. That rise is the price of the first slot: at most 3.2% on price-sensitive models, 14% on GPT-4o mini, and over 80% on the price-blind Nova Micro and Llama-3.1-8B (this control covers a wider price range than the main sweep; details are in the paper's Appendix D). This is a warning for every method that reads preferences by "asking a large model to pick one of two", including the common practice of "using a large model as a judge".

Wording matters less than the choice of line. The authors had a model rewrite one product's description truthfully 12 times, each version keeping the strong "best-seller" and "scarcity" lines. On GPT-4o the PE of these 12 versions ranged from 2.3% to 8.0%. Wording can be tuned, but far less than switching to a different kind of line (0.7% to 21.4%). On 5 pairs of headphones the authors also used PE to pick the most valuable of 9 lines in advance, then retested it on new product pairs: it beat the average of the 9 by 13.3 percentage points. So PE is not just a description after the fact; it can be used to choose lines beforehand, which makes it useful to regulators and also to sellers who want to manipulate agents.

Finally the authors tested Jev. This is a model built for decisions: it does not generate text but gives each option a probability of being chosen. The "ceiling" problem appears here too: four lines were all chosen at equal price, yet once priced they spread from 1.5% to 16.6%. This shows the ceiling problem is not limited to models that generate text. But its reactions differ from every chat model: "lots of people bought it" only works at the strongest level (15.4%); "expert recommended" is worth only 1.5%, against 19.8% on GPT-4o; "9 keep it" has no effect at all. The input format also changes the result: passing the product information as structured data instead of a paragraph of text raised the strong "best-seller" line from 2.0% to 10.8%.

## 5. Five practices the authors give auditors

The authors condense their experience into five rules that can be followed directly.

1. Balance position in every batch of trials: let the cued product take turns being first and second, and attach the cue to each of the two products in turn.
2. Look at the equal-price choice share first and use it as a two-sided check: if every line sits around 50%, the model is not really doing the task; if it is exactly 100%, this ruler can no longer show differences and you must switch to price.
3. Always include a price-only control, because PE is the ratio of "the line's pull" to "sensitivity to price".
4. Clearly label values that cannot be measured exactly ("at most 0" or "at least 26%") and leave them out of rankings.
5. When reading PE, trust the order and the rough band, not percentages to the decimal.

## 6. Limitations and practical meaning

This is a controlled pick-one-of-two experiment. It measures "how easily one sentence sways a model in a clean setting" and cannot directly predict real shopping. In real settings the line competes for attention with search results, reviews and multi-step browsing. The paper's claim that "models are not like people" is only a comparison with existing persuasion research; no humans did the same task. Scarcity was tested with one wording only, so a low PE only means this line did not work, not that models are immune to scarcity. Each category has only 6 product pairs, both categories are durable consumer electronics, and services such as travel and lodging are untested. The models were the ones at hand, and the conclusions hold only for them.

The authors also admit the tool cuts both ways: regulators can use it to audit, and sellers can use it to optimise copy aimed at agents. The line they draw is truthfulness: every cue is a sentence that is true of the product. Logs, test materials and code are public, but there is no ready-made library of "copy that best fools agents".

For teams building shopping agents and e-commerce platforms, there are three direct lessons. First, when evaluating whether an agent can be swayed by seller copy, do not look only at choice share; add a price axis, otherwise the strong lines all pile up at 100% and cannot be separated. Second, ==being listed first is itself a channel the platform controls and that can be priced==, so ranking policies deserve the same audit as product copy. Third, do not carry an audit result from one model over to another; first measure how sensitive it is to price. The code and data are open source and can be rerun directly on your own models and categories.

papers.title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
papers.authors: Farnoosh Hashemi, Shiyu Ji, Joice Chen, Michael W. Macy
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.
papers.summary: What happens when a group of LLM agents recommend songs to one another and each can see how many times a song has already been recommended? The authors reran the classic Music Lab experiment from sociology with songs the agents had never heard: one group could see the running recommendation counts, the other could not. The group that could see them quickly piled onto a few songs, and which song became a hit was close to luck, less and less related to how good the song was. Compared with humans in the same experiment, the models were more prone to herding and, once off course, found it hard to correct themselves. When multiple agents recommend or rate each other, letting them see popularity is risky.

papers.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
papers.authors: Asal Mehrabi, Mohammad Aliannejadi, Clemencia Siro
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
papers.summary: When LLMs act as judges scoring multilingual outputs, people often reuse what works in English, such as asking the judge to write out its reasoning first or to play an expert. The authors tried 9 prompting styles on 4 judge models across 27 languages and found that this experience does not transfer. Which judge model you use matters far more than how you prompt it. The same style can help one judge and hurt another. In low-resource languages the results are even less stable, and looking only at average scores hides all of this. The conclusion is simple: re-validate prompting choices on your own judge model and languages.
